entities.name: Cleopatra Selene II
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cleopatra Selene II, born in 40 BCE in Alexandria, Egypt, was a pivotal Ptolemaic princess whose life bridged the final collapse of the Hellenistic kingdoms and the consolidation of Roman imperial power under Augustus. As the only daughter of Cleopatra VII of Egypt and Mark Antony, she embodied the dynastic ambitions of two of the Roman Republic's most powerful figures, inheriting a complex political legacy. Her significance lies in her unique position as a surviving child of the losing side of the Roman Civil Wars, subsequently adopted into the Augustan household, and later established as Queen of Mauretania, where she became a crucial instrument of Roman policy in North Africa, facilitating cultural and economic integration between the Roman core and its frontier provinces.

Following the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE and the subsequent suicides of her parents in 30 BCE, the orphaned Selene, along with her brothers Alexander Helios and Ptolemy Philadelphus, was brought to Rome. She was paraded in Octavian's triumph in 29 BCE, a stark symbol of Rome's conquest of Egypt, before being raised in the household of Octavia the Younger, Octavian's sister and her late father's former wife. Around 25 BCE, Augustus strategically arranged her marriage to Juba II, a Numidian prince also raised in Rome, whom he appointed client king of Mauretania. Together, they founded the city of Caesarea (modern Cherchell, Algeria) and transformed their kingdom into a prosperous, Hellenized-Roman hub. Selene actively co-ruled, influencing Mauretanian administration, culture, and architecture, minting coins that depicted her with symbols of both Egyptian heritage and Roman authority, such as the crescent moon and cornucopia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cleopatra Selene II played a crucial role in stabilizing and Romanizing Mauretania, a key North African client kingdom, for over two decades, contributing to the broader Augustan peace and economic integration of the western Mediterranean.
